summary: Defines a way for a DHCPv6 relay agent to give the server information that the server can pass on to the client, since relays cannot talk directly to clients. It also updates RFC 3315 by making explicit that relays must not modify the encapsulated payloads they forward back toward clients.

plainLanguage.summary: A DHCP relay stands between a device and the address server and cannot talk to the device directly. This RFC gives the relay a way to hand a piece of information to the server and have the server pass it on to the device in its reply.

subtitle: A DHCPv6 option that lets a relay agent ask the server to pass an option on to the client.

tldr.problem: A DHCPv6 relay agent sometimes knows something the server does not, such as the local domain name used for EAP re-authentication, and the client may need it. DHCPv6 had no way for the relay to offer an option to the server.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Relay-Supplied Options option, code 66, that the relay puts in the Relay-Forward message and the server may copy into the reply sent to the client. Only options explicitly marked as RSOO-enabled may travel this way.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from December 2011 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3315 to make explicit that a relay must not modify the payload it forwards back to the client.

today: RFC 6422 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2011, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3315 by making explicit that relay agents must not modify the payload they forward back toward clients, and it leaves the list of options allowed inside the RSOO to be maintained by IANA.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 specification of RFC 3315 allows DHCP relay agents to forward DHCPv6 messages between clients and servers that are not on the same IPv6 link. In some cases the relay agent has information that is not available to the DHCP server but that would be useful to provide to the client. For example, the DHCP client may need to learn the EAP Re-authentication Protocol local domain name of RFC 6440, used for EAP re-authentication under RFC 5296, which is known to the relay agent but not to the server.

The DHCPv6 protocol specification does not provide a mechanism whereby the relay agent can provide options to the client. This document extends DHCP with a mechanism that allows relay agents to propose options for the server to send to DHCP clients.

The RFC is careful about its scope. It is not intended to provide a general mechanism for storing client configuration information in the relay agent. It is intended to address specific use cases where only the relay agent has information needed by the client. The extension is not applicable to DHCP options in general, but is provided as a mechanism for new specifications that require this functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a narrow extension, not a general way to configure clients from a relay. Each option has to be named one at a time as allowed to travel this way, and no existing DHCPv6 option is.

sections.title: Encoding
sections.content:
To supply options for the server to send to the client, the relay agent sends a Relay-Supplied Options option, abbreviated RSOO, in the Relay-Forward message. That option encapsulates whatever options the relay agent wishes to provide to the DHCPv6 server.

The option has three parts. The OPTION_RSOO field carries the Relay-Supplied Options code, 66. The option-length field carries the length of the RSOO. The options field carries one or more DHCPv6 options.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay wraps the options it wants to offer in a single DHCPv6 option with the number 66. The server sees that wrapper and knows where to look inside it.

sections.title: Which Options May Travel This Way
sections.content:
The RSOO must not contain any option that is not specifically called out as an RSOO-enabled option. Specifications that describe RSOO-enabled options must reference this specification and must state that the option they define is RSOO-enabled. No DHCP option specified prior to the issuance of this specification is RSOO-enabled.

A current list of RSOO-enabled options is kept by IANA in the registry titled Options Permitted in the Relay-Supplied Options Option. DHCP option specifications that define RSOO-enabled options must add text to their IANA Considerations section asking IANA to add the name of the option to that registry, in place of the words random relay option in the template the RFC gives.
sections.plainLanguage: Only options that have been explicitly approved for this path may be put in the wrapper. The list of approved ones is kept by IANA, and a new option has to be added there before a relay may send it.

sections.title: DHCP Relay Agent Behavior
sections.content:
Relay agents may include an RSOO in the option payload of a Relay-Forward message being sent toward a DHCP server. When relaying the payload of Relay-Reply messages toward clients, relay agents must not modify the payload. Relay agents must not send non-RSOO-enabled options in the Relay-Supplied Options option.

To allow network administrators to control the flow of RSOO options onto the network, relay agents that implement the Relay-Supplied Options option need a configuration parameter that determines whether they relay Relay-Forward messages containing RSOOs. A relay agent that has this parameter and is configured to disable forwarding of a Relay-Forward message containing an RSOO must silently discard any such message. Implementations that can be configured in this way must examine all Relay-Forward encapsulations, not just the outer one, because a relay agent may itself be nested inside another relay agent's message.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay can be told not to pass these messages on at all, and when it is told that it must drop them without telling anyone. It has to look inside nested relay messages too, not just the outermost one.

sections.title: DHCP Server Behavior
sections.content:
DHCP servers that implement this specification must examine each option contained in an RSOO to see whether it is an RSOO-enabled option, and must silently discard any option in an RSOO that is not. Server implementations should have an administrator-configurable list of RSOO-enabled options, so that new RSOO-enabled options do not require the software to be updated.

DHCP servers normally construct a list of options that are candidates to send to the client, and then construct the DHCP packet according to Section 17.2.2 of the DHCPv6 specification. If the server receives an RSOO it should add any options in it for which it has no internal candidate to that list of candidates. It should discard any option in the RSOO for which it already has one or more candidates. Aside from that addition, the server then constructs the DHCP packet as it normally would and transmits it to the client.

DHCP servers may receive multiply-nested Relay-Forward messages containing conflicting values for options contained in RSOOs. When such a conflict exists the server must choose no more than one of those options to forward to the client, and must not forward more than one. By default the server must choose the innermost value, the value supplied by the relay agent closest to the DHCP client. Server implementations may provide other heuristics for choosing which one of a set of conflicting options to forward, as long as the specified behaviour is the default.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks each relayed option against its approved list and drops anything not on it. It uses a relayed option only when it has nothing of its own for that option. When two relays in a chain supply different values for the same option, the server picks one, and by default that is the one from the relay nearest the client.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document provides a mechanism whereby a relay agent can inject options into the response the DHCP server sends to the DHCP client. In the currently known use cases, such as the ERP Local Domain Option of RFC 6440, RSOO-enabled options are options that will only ever originate on a relay agent and do not make sense when originating on a DHCP server. If some new RSOO-enabled option is specified that can originate from either the server or the relay agent, the RFC says this should be addressed in the security considerations of the document that specifies the use of that option.

In some environments there is an interface with a client and zero or more routers on one side, and a network managed by a monolithic or effectively monolithic administrative entity on the other. The nodes and routers on the client side are not controlled by that entity and are considered untrusted, while those on the network side are considered trusted.

It is possible for a malicious node acting as a relay agent on the untrusted side to supply an RSOO containing options that would override the same options provided by a relay agent on the trusted side. Where this is possible, network administrators are advised to use relay agents capable of dropping Relay-Forward messages containing the RSOO, and to configure them to do so. The RFC notes that this is only effective if the message from the DHCP server to the client is authenticated as specified in Section 21 of RFC 3315, or by some similar mechanism. Without that authentication, the malicious node can simply modify the server's response in transit back to the client, and there is no way for the client to detect it.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay near the client is under the control of whoever owns the client, not the network operator, and it could lie about an option. The advice is to configure relays to drop these messages, and to authenticate the server's reply, because otherwise a modified reply cannot be detected at all.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has assigned one new DHCPv6 option code from the registry of DHCP Option Codes. The option code 66, OPTION_RSOO, has been assigned to the Relay-Supplied Options option.

IANA has created a new registry on the same assignments page, titled Options Permitted in the Relay-Supplied Options Option. This registry enumerates the set of all code points from the DHCP Option Codes table for options that may appear in the RSOO. Options may be added to the list after IETF Review under the process of RFC 5226. When adding options, the description for the code added must match the description in the DHCP Option Codes table for that code, and option codes that have not been requested to be added should not be mentioned at all in the table, and should not be listed as reserved or unassigned.

IETF Review should include careful consideration of the security implications of allowing a relay agent to provide a value for the option being considered for addition to the registry. Where an IETF working group chartered to review DHCP protocol extensions exists, it is not sufficient for some other working group to review the registry addition.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps two lists here: the DHCPv6 option numbers, and the subset of them allowed inside the relay-supplied wrapper. Adding to the second list needs an IETF review that looks at the security consequences, not just a name check.
